# Purpose and central argument

Data analysis is not complete when a number has been calculated. A reader also needs to know which data were used, how they were transformed, why analytical choices were made, and what the result can support. When code, output, and explanation live in separate files, changes can leave a report displaying outdated values. Literate programming addresses this coordination problem by treating a program as something written for people as well as machines [@knuth1984]. In contemporary analysis, an executable document can place narrative, code, and results together.

This handout explains how Quarto implements that workflow and illustrates it with a simulated customer-churn analysis. Reproducible-paper workflows written with RStudio and Quarto provide a practical model for connecting method and narrative [@bauer2023]. The argument is deliberately limited: an executable document improves traceability, but it does not make weak data or unjustified conclusions reliable. Reproducibility requires the data, code, assumptions, software context, and interpretation to be sufficiently documented [@peng2009; @gandrud2020].

# Quarto as an analytical publishing workflow

A Quarto source file (`.qmd`) combines a YAML front matter block, Markdown, and optional executable code cells. YAML specifies document-wide metadata and output settings. Markdown structures prose with headings, lists, links, and tables. An R cell is fenced with `{r}` and can include options such as `echo: true` to show code or `eval: false` to skip execution. These are presentation and execution controls; hiding code does not remove it from the source.

Quarto is a publishing system, not a statistical package. During rendering, Quarto processes the source and coordinates execution through an engine; for R, a common engine is knitr. R performs the calculations, while Quarto converts the combined content to formats such as HTML, PDF, or slides [@quarto]. RStudio is an integrated development environment that helps a writer edit the source, run code, inspect files, and invoke rendering. The same project can also be rendered from a terminal, so the IDE is useful but not a requirement.

A minimal header illustrates configuration:

```yaml
---
title: "Customer churn"
format: html
bibliography: references.bib
csl: apa.csl
---
```

The source below the header can contain an executable R chunk. When the document is rendered, its output is recalculated from current inputs. Rendering is therefore a build step, not a guarantee: users should check that code ran, paths resolved, citations appeared, and the layout is readable. PDF generation additionally depends on a LaTeX engine and suitable fonts and packages.

Quarto uses Pandoc citation syntax with a BibTeX database and a Citation Style Language file. For example, `[@knuth1984]` produces an in-text citation, and the bibliography is generated from cited keys rather than typed into the document. Here `references.bib` stores source metadata and `apa.csl` supplies APA 7 formatting. Automation reduces repetitive formatting errors but cannot validate whether an author, date, DOI, or interpretation is correct; bibliographic metadata still requires checking [@hubercourse].

# Reproducibility and project practice

An executable report links a result to the steps that created it. This makes changes easier to review and can reduce transcription errors. A project should nevertheless preserve inputs, document data provenance and cleaning rules, use relative file paths, record software and package requirements, and avoid relying on a hidden interactive session. Version control makes edits and their history inspectable; it does not freeze an environment or make private inputs available to another reader. Reproducibility also differs from replication with new data: rerunning the same workflow checks computational consistency, whereas a new dataset or study asks whether findings extend beyond the original inputs [@peng2009; @gandrud2020].

This project keeps its generated CSV, deterministic R data-generation script, analysis source, exercise, bibliography, CSL, and rendered files in a clear folder structure. The example is explicitly simulated. Its data-generating rules are transparent and repeatable, but its outputs are teaching material rather than evidence about real telecommunications customers.

# Customer churn and revenue risk example

The business question is which customer segments show higher cancellation rates and which represent greater recurring-revenue exposure. One row represents a subscriber. Fields include contract type, tenure, support-contact count, monthly charge, and churn status. The R workflow imports the CSV with `readr`, inspects dimensions and missingness, standardizes categories, imputes missing monthly charges using the median within contract type, and records the imputation count. It then creates tenure bands and a binary churn flag. A grouped `dplyr` summary calculates segment sizes, churn rates, and the monthly charges belonging to churned accounts; `ggplot2` charts rates and revenue. These package roles are part of the broader tidyverse ecosystem [@wickham2019].

The following executable summary makes the denominator explicit and produces the segment table from the included CSV.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-contract-churn
#| tbl-cap: "Customer counts, churn rates, and observed churned monthly recurring revenue by contract type (simulated data)"
library(readr)
library(dplyr)

raw_customers <- read_csv("data/customer_churn_simulated.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
contract_medians <- raw_customers |>
  group_by(contract) |>
  summarise(contract_median = median(monthly_charge, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

customers <- raw_customers |>
  left_join(contract_medians, by = "contract") |>
  mutate(
    monthly_charge = if_else(is.na(monthly_charge), contract_median, monthly_charge),
    churn_flag = as.integer(churn == "Yes"),
    monthly_revenue = monthly_charge
  )

by_contract <- customers |>
  group_by(contract) |>
  summarise(
    customers = n(),
    churned = sum(churn_flag),
    churn_rate = mean(churn_flag),
    churned_mrr = sum(monthly_revenue[churn_flag == 1]),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
knitr::kable(by_contract, digits = 2,
             col.names = c("Contract", "Customers", "Churned",
                           "Churn rate", "Churned MRR (USD)"))
```

```{r}
#| label: rate-intervals
#| include: false
# 95% confidence intervals for two segment rates, used in the text below
ci_for <- function(k) {
  row <- by_contract[by_contract$contract == k, ]
  ci <- prop.test(row$churned, row$customers)$conf.int
  list(n = row$customers,
       txt = sprintf("%.0f%% to %.0f%%", 100 * ci[1], 100 * ci[2]))
}
ci_two <- ci_for("Two year")
ci_one <- ci_for("One year")
```


@tbl-contract-churn reports the segment denominator, churn count, churn rate, and monthly charges associated with churn. `group_by(contract)` defines the segments. Inside `summarise()`, `n()` counts all customers in the segment and the mean of a zero/one flag equals the churn proportion. The monthly charge total answers a separate financial question. Reporting both measures and the group size prevents a rate from being read without its scale.

In the fixed-seed sample, 72 of 330 month-to-month customers are marked as churned (21.8%); the corresponding rates are 12 of 173 one-year customers (6.9%) and 10 of 97 two-year customers (10.3%). After the documented imputation, the month-to-month group also has the largest observed monthly charge total associated with churn ($4,712). These figures are generated by the included simulation rules and should not be interpreted as evidence about an actual operator. One detail illustrates why group size matters: the two-year rate is higher than the one-year rate, although the generating script assigns two-year contracts a lower churn propensity. With only `r ci_two$n` two-year customers, approximate 95% confidence intervals for the two rates (`r ci_two$txt` and `r ci_one$txt`, computed with `prop.test()`) overlap widely, so the ordering of these two segments is sampling noise rather than a finding.

Missingness deserves its own check. The example deliberately blanks 18 of 600 monthly charges. Filling them with a contract-specific median allows the group revenue summaries to include these rows, but the imputed values are estimates, not recovered bills. A business analysis should examine why charges are missing and test whether missingness differs by churn status or customer segment. If the missingness is systematic, a simple median can bias the comparison; reporting the count and rule makes that limitation visible.

The two visual summaries serve different purposes: a bar chart of rates answers which group has the greater proportion, while an exposure chart puts the amount into a business scale. Figures should identify the measure, segment, and unit. Here the prices are simulated USD solely for the example. The scenario estimate multiplies active monthly revenue by the historical segment churn rate, assuming that rate applies to current active customers. It is useful for comparing rough priorities, but it is not a calibrated prediction, lifetime-value calculation, or causal estimate.

For segment `g`, the observed churn rate is

$$
\widehat{p}_g = \frac{\text{customers marked churned in }g}{\text{all observed customers in }g}.
$$

The denominator matters: comparing raw churn counts would favor large groups even if their rates were lower. Revenue measures answer a different question. The sum of monthly charges among churned accounts is a descriptive estimate of recurring monthly revenue associated with observed cancellations. It is not necessarily realized accounting loss: billing periods, partial months, discounts, and replacement customers are not modeled.

The example also reports a simple next-period scenario: active monthly revenue in a segment multiplied by its historical segment churn rate. This translates a rate into a rough exposure estimate, but assumes the prior rate applies to active accounts and is not a calibrated forecast. It should be labeled as an illustration and refreshed with a clearly defined time window in real operations.

A decision-maker should compare rate, segment size, and revenue together. A small group can have a high rate but little total exposure; a large group with a moderate rate may have more revenue at stake. The results can support prioritizing further investigation, such as reviewing service complaints or designing a retention experiment. They cannot show that contract type or support contacts caused cancellation. Such claims require a credible research design and evidence addressing confounding and selection. If an intervention is proposed, a controlled test with a defined outcome is more informative than treating descriptive associations as causal effects.

# Conclusion

Quarto makes it practical to keep analysis, explanation, and publication in one version-controlled project. YAML configures the document, Markdown communicates the reasoning, R cells compute results, and a bibliography plus CSL automates citation formatting. This workflow supports transparent review when inputs and decisions are documented. It does not replace subject knowledge, data validation, or critical interpretation. In the churn example, the most defensible output is a transparent description of simulated segment differences and a cautious proposal for what to test next.
